defects.summary: Every persistent-reservation command wrapper in pal/linux/kern.c retries a UNIT ATTENTION and then discards it: the sense data is never classified and nothing is signalled upward. A target raises UA on the other initiators precisely to tell them the PR state they believe in has changed (SPC-4: 2Ah/03h RESERVATIONS PREEMPTED, 2Ah/04h RESERVATIONS RELEASED, 2Ah/05h REGISTRATIONS PREEMPTED, 29h/xx POWER ON or RESET). MXFS throws that notification away and waits for its own next scheduled poll, so a node that is not the elected PR-health maintainer learns of a reservation loss only at its slow audit -- and that interval is time the cluster cannot fence a peer death. The sess381 design ruling required event-driven checks 'at mount, on any unmount anomaly, on a target reset / Unit Attention, and unconditionally in the fencing path before a PREEMPT'; the UA trigger is the one item of that list never built.
defects.evidence: CODE FACT, verifiable by grep: 'grep -n UNIT_ATTENTION pal/linux/kern.c' returns a separate bounded retry loop per command -- the PR OUT preempt-and-abort path ~3756, REPORT CAPABILITIES ~3842, the PR IN wrappers ~4551 and ~4984, and the data-path READ passthrough ~683 and ~1379. Each tests only sense_key == UNIT_ATTENTION, sleeps and reissues; none reads asc/ascq, and no classification of asc/ascq for PR purposes exists anywhere in the tree. There is no single PAL funnel for PR commands, so the retry loops are per-command; and dlm/ must still build in user mode, so any signal has to cross that boundary as a registered callback or an out-parameter, never a direct call into SCSI code. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, 2-node TCP rig 2026-09-17, build E927E501A55C222725566A8, tests/evidence/sess41_d0381/armA_FIXED_E927E501.log: after an out-of-band release of the reservation, the stand-in node's repair landed at t+62 s, of which only the last 20.50 s was its deliberate takeover deadline. The other ~42 s was purely waiting for its own 60 s audit to come round, while the target had already raised a UA it could have acted on at once. With the repair-authority half fixed in 0.86.2, detection latency is now the dominant term in how long an MXFS cluster stays unfenceable after a reservation loss.
defects.next: DESIGN CONSULT ALREADY HELD (Astra, 2026-09-17); its hazards must be answered before coding, not after. (1) A UA is PENDING SENSE, not a push: nothing is delivered until some command exposes it, so instrumenting only the PR wrappers may not help an idle node AT ALL -- an auditor's next PR command is the very audit the trigger was meant to accelerate. MEASURE FIRST where a UA is actually observed, including whether the SCSI midlayer consumes and retries it on ordinary data I/O before MXFS ever sees it. (2) Do not treat all of ASC 2Ah as the PR-relevant class (it carries unrelated changes), but do not whitelist exact codes only either -- a coarse or vendor-specific code for the same event would be silently uncovered. Preferred: definite PR/reset codes take a fast lane; an unrecognised UA invalidates the cached state and schedules a coalesced, bounded check, with counters and rate-limited diagnostics. (3) 2Ah/05h REGISTRATIONS PREEMPTED is evidence about the OBSERVING nexus's own registration and belongs in the existing fenced-self inspection path, not the ordinary auditor delay; receiving it is not the same as a completed inspection. (4) Separate the two actions: logical cache invalidation must be IMMEDIATE at notification time, or a fencing path can consume the stale snapshot meanwhile, while target interrogation stays asynchronous (a synchronous PRIN from a heartbeat or data-path thread is the wrong default). Guard the race where a check already in flight clears a dirty flag set after it started -- use a sequence number, not a boolean, and account for the check's OWN UA retry generating the callback. (5) A PR-relevant UA met INSIDE a PREEMPT or PREEMPT-AND-ABORT retry loop must not be transparently retried: it may mean the assumptions established before the fence began are now stale, so return revalidate/restart rather than hiding it. (6) At 32 nodes jitter alone is insufficient -- coalesce a burst into ONE pending obligation whose deadline later events may advance but never push out, rate-limit executions with at most one check in flight per LU, and keep UNKNOWN as UNKNOWN rather than letting backoff turn it into a stale OK. (7) A reset UA (29h) does NOT imply lost registrations: PRs are meant to survive resets distinct from power loss, so it must never clear software registration state or trigger a REGISTER. TESTS the consult says this patch must pass, beyond re-running the two existing arms in tests/resv_health_detect.sh and tests/resv_selfgone_withdraw.sh: idle victim, with time-to-first-UA-observation measured SEPARATELY from observation-to-inspection; a UA consumed on ordinary I/O, proving whether the callback sees it at all; a notification arriving during a successful check, proving it is not cleared by that check; a UA storm, proving a bounded command rate and no deadline starvation; total PR loss, proving the maintainer does not automatically REGISTER itself; and a reset with PR retained, proving no false withdrawal. RELATED: the repair-authority half of this area was fixed and verified in 0.86.2 -- a stand-in now takes the repair over when the elected maintainer is gone -- and this record is ONLY the event-driven trigger.
defects.impact_why: Pace of fencing repair: after an out-of-band reservation release the stand-in's repair landed at t+62 s, about 42 s of it waiting for the 60 s audit (tests/evidence/sess41_d0381/armA_FIXED_E927E501.log); the reservation was repaired, nothing corrupted, hung or shut down. A data effect needs a second independent fault (a peer death whose zombie I/O lands) inside that window, which the record does not show; it stays in the queue as a fencing-latency defect.

defects.summary: Two nodes alternating aligned 4 KiB O_DIRECT writes into one shared file with a 20000-extent, two-level extent tree (about 97 bmbt blocks) complete about 425 writes per node in 90 s (4.7 writes/s each), against about 15000 per node in 90 s on a 16-block file under the same contention; and a buffered read (cat) of that 4 GiB sparse file on one node while the peer writes into it does not finish inside 90 s. Every grant handoff on a btree-format file re-reads the tree cold: the reload evicts every cached bmbt block the inode owns (P59-BMBT-EVICT, bmbt_evict=1000 capped per lap) and the next extent load re-reads all of them (iomap_iread_pr 425-528 per lap), so the cost of a handoff grows with the tree, not with the write.
defects.evidence: tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh on build 8E4C6A2CC5EAC566F5438FD (0.87.5), 2/tcp: NOCAT=1 EXTEND=1 EXTSPAN=1048576 PREFILL=20000 90 s lap (tests/evidence/20260918T041101Z_dwcd_fin_hugenc) test1 'WRITER ok=428 failed=0', test2 'ok=425 failed=0', iomap_iread_pr=425 on each, bmbt_evict=1000 (cap) on each, rel_bmbt_flushed 1/3; the same lap with the preamble read (20260918T040220Z_dwcd_fin_huge): test1 'WRITER ok=0 failed=0' because its cat of the 4 GiB file ran the whole 90 s window (iomap_iread_pr=528) while test2 wrote 2749; the 65536-block span lap (035930Z_dwcd_fin_deep) likewise test1 ok=0 (cat, iomap_iread_pr=736), test2 4567. The 16-block aligned lap on the same build: 14818/14999 writes in 90 s.
defects.next: Measure what one handoff of the 97-block tree costs, stage by stage (reload eviction walk, extent load reads, release scan) with the per-release timing line, and compare with a handoff that keeps the cached blocks that a peer did not change (a per-block generation or a release-time list of blocks this tenure wrote, so the reload evicts only what changed). A buffered reader should not have to re-acquire per mapping while a writer extends the file: consider a PR tenure that survives a peer's EX for the read window, or readahead that maps in larger chunks under one grant.
defects.impact_why: pace only: no write failed, no image differed, nothing hung past the lap; the 2/tcp release bar excludes pace

defects.summary: A stat whose inode acquire the recovery-blocked cutoff aborted with EIO (P240-RBLK-EIO-ABORT: the grant is held by a dead node in RECOVERY_BLOCKED) still reached mxfs_getattr_dlm_unlock, and the DLM end found no holder to pair with: P71-UNDERFLOW ino=128 mode=PR state=0 dlm_mode=0 un=mxfs_getattr_dlm_unlock. Either mxfs_ilock_fallible returned 0 (locked) for an acquire that mxfs_dlm_ilock_begin had abandoned at -EHOSTDOWN, or the abort path cleared the holder accounting that the end expected; either way one end ran with no begin behind it, and an unpaired end on a shared inode is the class that can release a grant a live holder still uses.
defects.evidence: Measured 2026-09-18, 2 nodes / TCP, 0.87.14 sv 8C88197C64B31AB03AF342A, twice (2 of 2 laps of tests/d0356_stranded_prover_return.sh: tests/evidence/20260918T170833Z_d0356spr_s53d/A_journal.txt and 20260918T171956Z_d0356spr_s53e/A_journal.txt): during the unmount of a node whose standing fencing attempt the gate-refusal knob kept unprovable, 'P304-FENCE-BLOCKED-DURABLE slot=1' -> 'P240-RBLK-EIO-ABORT ino=128 mode=3 comm=umount' -> 'P71-UNDERFLOW ino=128 mode=PR state=0 dlm_mode=0 comm=umount un=mxfs_getattr_dlm_unlock+0x13/0x20' -> 'P199-UNMOUNT-RESIDUAL-INODE ino=128 icount=2' -> 'P-SB-SUMMARY-FINAL-FAIL slot=0 lock_rc=-112'. The unmount completed (rc=0, 110-115 s), the departure was DIRTY by design, the returning peer replayed the slice and both witness files were intact; no fault, hang or shutdown on either lap. No P958-GETATTR-REFUSED line, so mxfs_getattr_dlm_lock did not see the abort as an error.
defects.next: PATCH IN TREE, UNBUILT (s59, tree at 0.87.22, module still 0FCDC94EE691B01E8B942F4 on the rig while the capture-gate sweep runs): (1) the -EHOSTDOWN arm of mxfs_dlm_ilock_begin (xfs_mxfs_dlm.c ~37815) now calls mxfs_acqfall_give_up_rc(ino, -EIO) when the task registered as fallible, the same shape as the transition-stall arm; (2) XFS_ILOCK_MXFS_NOEND (1u<<8, xfs_inode.h) tells xfs_iunlock no DLM end is owed, and mxfs_ilock_fallible releases its components with it on the give-up path. FOUND WHILE READING: every fallible give-up already left this signature — 'P71-UNDERFLOW mode=PR state=0 dlm_mode=0 un=mxfs_ilock_fallible' in 13 evidence captures (the blackhole laps s586d/s586h/s589a/s595a/s606h, md5sum and python3 readers) — because xfs_iunlock runs the end for every ILOCK/IOLOCK flag and the begin installed nothing; (2) closes that whole class at the boundary. NOT covered by this patch, stated: the other audited sites (xfs_vn_update_time, the ichange and attr transaction allocators, readdir, lookup) release through their callees' own xfs_iunlock without the flag, so a give-up there still prints one clamped, inert P71-UNDERFLOW; a choke-point check in the end hook would cost a task-hash lookup on every unlock, so it is left for a change of its own. VERIFY once the rig is free: make modules, deploy (MXFS_FORCE_PREP=1 ./run.sh 2 tcp prep_cluster), then tests/d0356_stranded_prover_return.sh 2 laps requiring P958-GETATTR-REFUSED rc=-5 after P240-RBLK-EIO-ABORT comm=umount and ZERO 'P71-UNDERFLOW.*un=mxfs_getattr_dlm_unlock' and ZERO 'un=mxfs_ilock_fallible'; then one tcp_lockreq_blackhole lap (ARMED_S=180) requiring zero 'un=mxfs_ilock_fallible' where s586h had them; then remove with --why.
defects.impact_why: Adjudicated from the code (0.87.21, xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c): the PR end decrements only when i_dlm_pr_holders > 0 (38700) and otherwise just counts and prints P71-UNDERFLOW (38714-38724); every release arm after the bookkeeping is gated on state BAST or CACHED (38749-38753, the idle reaper 38844) and the observed end ran at state=0 dlm_mode=0 (NONE/NL, the -EHOSTDOWN arm at 37815-37834 had reset the state and installed nothing), so nothing downstream can release or demote a grant. Measured: both laps' unmounts completed rc=0, replay intact, no hang, no shutdown. A stat that returns cached attributes under no grant is a coherency defect at a boundary designed to fail, not corruption or loss.

defects.summary: A node that unmounts cleanly and remounts in the same boot (the same derived PR key) while its peer is also mounting is fenced by that peer: the predecessor's heartbeat slot is released RETIRE_PENDING at put_super and umount returns, the successor re-registers the identical key 2.4 s later and takes over the PR-ledger entry, but its own settlement of the predecessor's record (P305-RETIRE-SETTLED-OWN) lands only 8.6 s after the release, behind register, reserve and the FENCECAP probe; the peer's mount thread sighted the record 0.1 s after the release, held its admission (P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD rc=1 WAITING) and at 9.7 s, its 10 s mount grace spent, preempt-and-aborted the key, naming the successor (P-PR-FENCE dead node 3432382203, P-VERGATE-FENCE slot=0 state=4). The successor's mount is refused (rc=32) and the predecessor's deferred release, unregistering 12 s after the slot release, finds the key gone and its ledger RETIRED write answered RESERVATION CONFLICT (P-PRKEY-RETIRED rc=-52). The unregister itself did not conflict; the conflict on the ledger write is the consequence of the peer's preempt. This is the s49ctl hazard the 0.87.11 mount-thread grace was designed to cover (a successor settles EMPTY within a second); measured, the successor's settle takes 8.6 s against a 10 s grace.
defects.evidence: tests/d0965_remount_bracket_race.sh healthy lap s58h-H22 on 0.87.19, tests/evidence/20260918T232955Z_d0965race_s58h-H22-d0965_remount_bracket_race-ok. test1 (A then A', lap1_test1.txt): 3251.887 P304-RETIRE-QUIESCED at=put_super submitted=6534; 3251.915 P304-RETIRE-PENDING-RELEASED slot 0; 3252.795 A' PREOBSERVE (mount start, 0.9 s after the release); 3254.355 P-PRKEY-REGISTERED key=0x702f116e501f9c5e keys=2 and P305-PR-SAME-BOOT-RETIRE-PENDING slot=0 node=3079361979; 3254.384 ledger idx=0 REGISTERED node=3432382203 (the successor took the entry); 3255.9-3257.4 P303-FENCECAP/OK; 3260.500 P305-RETIRE-SETTLED-OWN slot=0 proof=own-registration-bracket, P305-RETIRE-SETTLED 'mount proceeds' (8.6 s after the release); 3263.905 the old incarnation's deferred release unregisters (P-PR-DEPARTURE-UNHELD op=unregister, 12.0 s after the release); 3263.923 'sd 3:0:0:0: reservation conflict' then P-PRKEY-RETIRED idx=0 node=3432382203 rc=-52; lap1_amount.txt: mount rc=32 wall_ms=11188, P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD slot=0 rc=1. test2 (B', lap1_test2.txt, win_grace_6_test2.txt): 173.463 PREOBSERVE (its own mount start); 173.539 P274-CLAIM-RETIRE-PENDING-SKIP slot=0 node=3079361979 (first sight, <=0.1 s after A's release by the clock offset the release/sighting pair fixes); 174.948 P304-RETIRE-PENDING-SEEN slot=0 state=UNKNOWN; 174.990 P304-RETIRE-WORKER result=PRESENT (the successor's identical key); 175.240 P304-RETIRE-PRESENT-GRACE seen=290 ms ago and P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD slot=0 rc=1; 183.224 P-PR-FENCE preempt-and-aborted dead node 3432382203 (key 0x702f116e501f9c5e) gen=4464 EXCLUSION PROVED, P236-FENCEKIND kind=PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE(16), P-VERGATE-FENCE slot=0 node=3432382203 epoch=12367608096848124051 state=4 pr_fence=ok (9.7 s after first sight; MXFS_DISKLOCK_RETIRE_MOUNT_GRACE_MS=10000, dlm/disklock.h:128); BMOUNT rc=0 wall_ms=8864. Code: the successor's own settle is v5_p305_settle_retire_pending (dlm/v5_mount.c:3235, own-key arm 3268-3286) called from the mount at 14176/14652 after the PR context and the disklock exist; the predecessor's unregister is in the deferred release (v5_mount.c:15751, inside mxfs_v5_dlm_shutdown_defer_release at 15408) after peer shutdown, DLM destroy and the tauth ledger close, which is why it trails the slot release by 12 s. The same harness passed s57b-11 (0.87.19, tests/evidence/laps_s57/): the race has a ~1 s margin and does not always lose.
defects.next: 1. DESIGN CONSULT before any change (fencing semantics, hard to reverse): the successor re-registers the identical per-boot key before it can settle the predecessor's RETIRE_PENDING record, so for the whole register-to-settle window (measured 6.1 s: 3254.4 to 3260.5) the record reads PRESENT to every peer and the peer's grace is the only thing standing between the successor and a preempt of its live key. Shapes to bring: (a) settle the own-boot record BEFORE re-registering the key, when READ KEYS can prove the key ABSENT (the predecessor's deferred release must then unregister before umount returns, or the successor must wait for it: mxfs_v5_dlm_departure_lock already serializes 'same-boot re-registration against the old unmount's late phase'); (b) move the own-settle ahead of the FENCECAP probe so the window shrinks to the register itself; (c) a peer whose sync lookup finds the key PRESENT with the same host+boot identity as the record and a ledger entry already REGISTERED to a NEWER node id treats it as a successor in progress and extends its grace rather than withdrawing. 2. Reproduce on demand: tests/d0965_remount_bracket_race.sh test1 test2 3 <label>, and stamp the successor's register-to-settle window (P-PRKEY-REGISTERED to P305-RETIRE-SETTLED-OWN) and the peer's first-sight-to-fence window on every lap. 3. Fix at the proven cause, then three laps with the successor never fenced and the predecessor's ledger RETIRED write rc=0.
defects.impact_why: Availability, not integrity or stability: the predecessor quiesced and released before the successor existed (P304-RETIRE-QUIESCED submitted=6534, then the slot release), the successor was fenced at admission before it went writable (its mount refused rc=32, no I/O of its own in flight), the peer mounted (rc=0) and nothing crashed, hung or shut down on either node in the lap. What it costs is a same-boot remount that races a peer's mount; it stays in the queue as a fencing-design defect (a live successor fenced on its predecessor's record).

defects.summary: A live foreign-generation heartbeat writer on the shared LUN is invisible to MXFS and its slot is claimable: hb_gen_foreign classes any ACTIVE record whose fs_gen is not ours as a pre-mkfs ghost with no liveness test, the join gate and heartbeat monitor skip it with no log line, and mxfs_disklock_claim_slot treats it as claimable, so a host still running an old mxfs on the same LUN heartbeats (and, whenever the LUN is unreserved, writes its stale filesystem) into a live cluster's platter with nothing in any node's journal naming it.
defects.evidence: Measured s67 (2/tcp, QNAP LUN naa.6e843b6393a5a6ed918bd4f4fdb8e7d6): with both rig VMs torn down (mxfs unloaded), slot 2 carried an ACTIVE record node=1216714748 fs_gen=0 epoch=0 pr_key=0 whose ts_ms advanced 2016 ms per dump interval (tests/evidence/20260919T134608Z_foreign_writer_serv_s67/). The writer was serv.localdomain 192.168.1.5: Debian 5.10.0-45, the physical-campaign DKMS mxfs.ko (2026-05), /etc/fstab _netdev mount of /dev/sdb at every boot, mounted 2026-09-17T18:46 CDT, 48027 mxfs kernel lines since. Its writes are fenced only by the cluster's SCSI reservation: a scratch WE-AR reservation from test1 froze the stamp for 6 s and the clear released it, and serv's journal shows 'heartbeat write failed: -52' bursts exactly in the reservation windows. In every unreserved window (mkfs, the gap before the first mount reserves, PR transitions) its heartbeat and its stale filesystem's writes land: the s62e mkfs zero_region verify FAIL ('K' of MXLK at the slot 2 sector) was this writer, misattributed for three sessions to 'a node from the previous lap'. Code: dlm/disklock.c hb_gen_foreign (line ~236) has no liveness term; the join gate at ~5434 and the claim loop at ~11440 skip/claim on that test alone; no P-line names a foreign-generation ACTIVE record. The rig-side fix (prep refuses under any advancing record, 0.89.4) closes the mkfs hole only; the module still admits a mount beside a live foreign writer silently.
defects.next: Design the liveness term with a consult: a foreign-generation ACTIVE record whose timestamp advances across the heartbeat interval is a LIVE FOREIGN WRITER, not a ghost — log it (slot, node, fs_gen, stamp delta) at the join gate and in the monitor, never claim its slot, and decide whether admission must refuse (the writer shares the platter; the reservation fences it during tenure but not across PR transitions) or proceed with the slot excluded. Prove with an injected writer: a second initiator stamping a foreign-gen record on a spare slot while the fleet mounts; assert the P-line, the slot skip, and the admission decision; then a claim attempt on that slot under a cleared reservation to show the collision the fix prevents.
defects.impact_why: It corrupts nothing and hangs nothing under the release configuration as measured: the cluster's WE-AR reservation blocks the foreign initiator's writes for the whole tenure (stamp frozen under a scratch reservation, EBADE bursts in serv's journal), and the rig-side guard now refuses to format under it. The exposure is the unreserved windows and the missing diagnostic, so it stays in the queue below the release bar.

defects.summary: The mount-time orphan sweep runs before the mount's recovery census and the join gate's declarations, so reclamation of departed authorities is attempted while this node has not yet reconstructed the platter's recovery obligations; the 0.89.4 platter-backed retention predicate closes the measured hole, but the ordering itself was ruled wrong: destructive maintenance should follow an inventory of ACTIVE occupancy and victim-to-obligation index, and the ACTIVE -> RECOVERY_GUARD -> released handoff should be stated and tested as an invariant with no durable gap.
defects.evidence: Design consult Astra 2026-09-19 on D-A-MOUNT-S-ORPHAN-SWEEP-RETIRES-THE-LEDGER-RECORDS (fixed at 0.89.4 by the platter-backed predicate, measured s67h/s67k): the consult's shape beyond the shipped change — (A) inventory before destructive maintenance: fs generation, read and validate the table, populate ACTIVE occupancy and a separate victim-to-obligation index, discover guards regardless of owner/lease/marker, schedule adoption of stranded attempts; (B) run the opportunistic sweep after that census and the join gate's classification, never before; (C) one retention rule at every destructive choke point immediately before the action; (D) release only by the recovery state machine's durable completion, never by age or owner change. Code: dlm/v5_mount.c v5_orphan_sweep_queue at mount (~14491) runs before the barrier's declarations; dlm/dlm.c dlm_orphan_scan dead test = occupant map + view. No failure measured after the 0.89.4 predicate (d0356 s67k, d0981 s67i, sole_survivor s67j, join_during_takeover s67m all PASS).
defects.next: Move the mount-time sweep behind the mount's recovery census (after the barrier's declarations and the stranded-attempt adoption), make the census seed the pending markers, and prove the sweep's ordering with the d0356 shape run with the sweep deliberately exercised before local declarations; state the ACTIVE->GUARD->released invariant in docs/tcp-authority-ledger.md and add the crash points around that handoff to the fence crash matrix.
defects.impact_why: Nothing measured fails after the 0.89.4 predicate: the retention rule at the choke point protects the records whatever the sweep's ordering. The ordering is a design hazard the consult named, not an observed corruption, hang or crash.

defects.summary: COMPARE AND WRITE is submitted to the SCSI midlayer with a retry allowance, so a CAW that already executed can be re-issued after error handling and then MISCOMPARE against the data it itself wrote - reporting a FALSE FAILURE for a compare-and-swap that in fact committed. Every disklock CAS in the tree rides this primitive.
defects.evidence: ESTABLISHED BY CODE INSPECTION, not yet measured. pal/linux/kern.c mxfs_pal_bdev_compare_and_write issues opcode 0x89 through scsi_execute_cmd(..., 30 * HZ, 1, &args); the penultimate argument is the midlayer RETRY COUNT, so the block layer may re-issue the CDB once on its own after error handling has aborted it, and the caller sees only one return value. COMPARE AND WRITE is not idempotent in the way a retry assumes: if the first execution applied the write and its response was lost or timed out, the re-issued command compares the caller's ORIGINAL expected image against the NEW on-platter contents, miscompares, and returns failure for an operation that succeeded. Found while auditing the same parameter on the PREEMPT AND ABORT wrapper for D-FENCE-POSTSUBMIT-AMBIGUITY-NO-RECONCILIATION-381, where the design consult's requirement is that 'no queued retry, retransmission, reinstatement or error-handling path can generate another execution-capable instance of the operation'. Every other passthrough in that file also carries retries=1; the reads and the FUA WRITE(16) are idempotent and unaffected. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which callers a false-negative CAS actually harms. The disklock protocol generally re-reads after a failed CAS, and the certificate-publication path was explicitly taught at 0.89.13 to treat a failed CAS as an UNKNOWN commit outcome, so some callers already tolerate it; the slot-claim, heartbeat and recovery-descriptor paths have not been audited against it.
defects.next: 1) Decide the retry count deliberately per command class rather than uniformly: a non-idempotent state-changing command needs retries=0 so that exactly one execution attempt happens per call and a lost response stays honestly UNKNOWN. 2) Before changing it, audit every caller of mxfs_pal_bdev_compare_and_write for what a FALSE FAILURE does - a caller that re-reads and reconciles is safe, a caller that treats failure as 'my write did not happen' is not, and that is the list this record needs. 3) Measure it rather than reasoning about it: the initiator-side shape is to correlate the passthrough and error-handler events with the target's command traffic, which does not need target instrumentation. 4) Do NOT fix this in the same change as the PREEMPT AND ABORT retry count - they are different commands with different callers and a shared patch makes neither result attributable.
defects.impact_why: DOES NOT CROSS THE 2-NODE TCP RELEASE BAR, and the earlier integrity classification was a fail-closed guess made when this was filed, not a measurement. What the code establishes: recov_cas_durable (dlm/disklock.c) returns the CAS failure and the caller RE-READS the descriptor and re-decides from the platter - its own comment states the contract, 'the recovery stays at its current stage (fail closed) and the caller re-decides'. Every disklock CAS is a read-modify-CAS loop over durable state, so a false-negative costs a retry, not correctness: the re-read sees whatever actually landed, including our own image. That is the same shape 0.89.13 formalised deliberately for the certificate path, where a failed CAS is treated as an UNKNOWN commit outcome. No path is known that turns a false negative into lost or corrupted data, and none that hangs or crashes a node. NOT DISPROVED, and it stays in the queue: the slot-claim callers (disklock.c:11496, :12750) have not been audited, and a node that believes it failed to claim a slot it in fact holds could strand that record. That audit is what this record is open for - it is not a release gate.

defects.summary: The bootstrap-owner takeover decides an owner is fenced from PR-LEDGER STATE and from a boot boundary, minting PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE or SELF_SUCCESSION_DONE without any target operation or retirement basis, and that kind is what authorises replacing the bootstrap owner.
defects.evidence: REACH CORRECTED 2026-09-20 (0.89.19), and this is the substantive finding: THE WHOLE-CLUSTER BOOTSTRAP IS A CAW PATH AND DOES NOT RUN ON TCP, so the producer this record is about cannot execute on the transport this release ships. Established by two laps and then by the call graph. LAPS: tests/bootstrap_takeover_2n.sh s86d and s86e (tests/evidence/20260920T140746Z_btk_s86d, 20260920T141955Z_btk_s86e) drove the shape the record's previous next step specified - both slices dirty, both nodes destroyed, one node back alone on 2/tcp. Neither reached a claim. In both, the mount read the record (P-BOOT-STATE IDLE), claimed an ORDINARY heartbeat slot 12 ms later, and then spent 122 s in the admission barrier running 116 and 155 inline replay rounds that each refused both slices, before the barrier refused the mount. CALL GRAPH: v5_boot_tk_fence_key is reached only from v5_bootstrap_takeover_run, which is reached only from v5_bootstrap_run, which has exactly ONE call site, dlm/v5_mount.c:16211 - and the TCP arm of mxfs_v5_dlm_init ends with 'return ctx' at :15990, so everything from :15993 ('CAW transport requires disklock region') is the CAW arm. The tree says so itself at :15653: 'the TCP transport carries its own durable authority ledger and no PR-fence bootstrap; the record is opened for the owner-liveness view only ... (bootstrap is a CAW path)'. WHAT TCP DOES STILL DO WITH THE RECORD: v5_bootstrap_setup opens it, the pre-register path reads it and can set boot_takeover_pending or boot_resume_pending - which nothing on TCP then consumes - and it REFUSES the mount with P-BOOT-ADMISSION-REFUSED-PREREGISTER (-EBUSY) for any state that is not IDLE or RECOVERY_COMPLETE. On a TCP-only volume the record never leaves the IDLE that mkfs writes, so this defect is unreachable there; on a volume that has ever been mounted with CAW, a non-IDLE record refuses every TCP mount with no TCP route to advance or clear it (and chk_mxfs --clear-bootstrap accepts only REFUSED, never CLAIMED). That cross-transport hazard is D-A-BOOTSTRAP-TAKEOVER-THAT-CANNOT-OBTAIN-A-RETIREMENT-PROOF-..., not this record. EVERYTHING PREVIOUSLY RECORDED HERE STANDS: the producer fix shipped in 0.89.16, the readers were exercised against every class in 0.89.17, and the bootstrap path itself is still undriven - it just has to be driven on CAW.
defects.next: RUN IT ON CAW — and this rig cannot, yet. The previous next step specified a 2-node TCP shape; that shape cannot reach the code (see the evidence: the whole-cluster bootstrap is in the CAW arm of mxfs_v5_dlm_init and the TCP arm returns before it). tests/bootstrap_takeover_2n.sh now defaults to MXFS_TRANSPORT=caw and refuses a tcp run up front with that reason, so the lap is written and ready. WHAT BLOCKS IT: run.sh:98 gives the caw transport DEV_DEFAULT=/dev/mapper/mpatha, which belongs to the OLD multipath/SCST rig; on this rig prep aborts in 15 s with 'FS_PREP_FAIL: /dev/mapper/mpatha is not a block device' (tests/evidence/20260920T143106Z_btk_s86f/prep.log, clyde_preflight PASS immediately before it, so the host is healthy and this is device selection alone). BEFORE RE-RUNNING: establish whether the shipping QNAP LUN implements SCSI COMPARE AND WRITE at all - tools/caw_verify against the transport self-test scratch sector answers it, and a node's P-TRANSPORT-CONFORMED line reports what the peers voted, not what the target supports. If it does, the lap runs as MXFS_DEV=/dev/sda MXFS_TRANSPORT=caw tests/bootstrap_takeover_2n.sh <label> both. If it does NOT, say so here: the bootstrap-owner path would then be unreachable on every transport this rig can run, and the record's disposition has to be argued from code with that stated, not from a lap that cannot exist. THE NON-VACUITY CONDITIONS AND THE ARMS ARE UNCHANGED and are in the harness header and docs/rulings/bootstrap-takeover-closure-and-the-recovery-dead-end.md: bind the pre-cut state to one owner boot and one term with TARGET-FACING PR IN evidence, capture the predicates the deleted branches would have read (the module now prints would_have_minted= on the refusal for exactly this), assert the absence of AUTHORITY of any class rather than the absence of kind 16, and grade an arm whose antecedent is 'none' as NOT REPRODUCING.
defects.impact_why: The kind is the sole authorisation for replacing a bootstrap owner, and the takeover proceeds to own cluster formation for the LUN. A previous owner whose accepted writes the target has not retired can land them after the new owner has taken the record, and the CAS protects against a stale-image write, not against a write the target already accepted. Filed at the integrity bar by inspection on the 2-node TCP path; it has not been measured, and the measurement in the next step decides whether it stays there.

defects.summary: A LOGICAL UNIT RESET issued by ANY initiator against the shared LUN strands, on every OTHER initiator, exactly the commands the target was holding at that instant - and each stranded command costs its owner 538 s before the SCSI error handler aborts and retries it. The retry succeeds and no data is lost. The id says HANGS FOREVER and that is wrong: measured, it recovers. What is real is a nine-minute stall of an application's I/O caused by an operation on another host.
defects.evidence: MEASURED 2026-09-20, tests/lu_reset_bystander_eh.sh s84h, 2-node TCP, build 36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343, fails=0, evidence tests/evidence/20260920T120749Z_lrbe_s84h. Ten resets six seconds apart from test1; test2 writing O_DIRECT into an MXFS file throughout at ~1600 writes/s. ONE of the ten stranded a command: the writer's progress counter froze at 107910 at t=60s and resumed at t=609s. 538 s stall, zero application errors, then normal throughput. THE MECHANISM, narrated by the stack itself once debug_libiscsi_eh and scsi logging_level 63 were armed on the bystander (both are OFF by default, which is why the earlier probe's silent kernel log proved nothing): timeouts=7 timer_reset=2 not_handled=1 aborts=3 device_resets=0, then 'sd 3:0:0:0: [sda] tag#73 aborting command', 'session1: iscsi_eh_abort abort success [sc ... itt 0x15]', 'sd 3:0:0:0: [sda] tag#73 retry aborted command'. 538 s is three expiries of the 180 s device command timeout plus the abort. The ladder is drivers/scsi/libiscsi.c iscsi_eh_cmd_timed_out: rung 1 'command making progress' resets the timer, rung 2 resets it if an older running task progressed, rung 3 sends a nop-out and resets it, and only the pass after that returns SCSI_EH_NOT_HANDLED and lets the error handler in. A SINGLE reset does not reproduce it at all - s84g, one reset, 109054 writes across it with zero errors and zero EH activity (tests/evidence/20260920T120303Z_lrbe_s84g): the target has to be holding one of this initiator's commands at the instant the task-management function executes. WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN, and this is what took it off the stability bar: zero fence, death-declaration, recovery-pending and self-withdraw lines in EITHER node's window across the whole 1114 s lap; no BUG, no Oops, no filesystem shutdown; both nodes answering. The peer never declared the stalled node dead even though the dead window is 62 s, because a LU reset strands only the tasks the target held at that instant - the heartbeat's own commands, issued afterwards, complete normally. The issuer wrote 217171 blocks with zero errors across the series, its own error handler failing and re-submitting its commands as designed. THE ORIGINAL READING IS FULLY EXPLAINED AND WAS WRONG IN TWO PLACES: it reasoned from a 30 s command timeout when the device's timeout is 180 s AND MXFS SETS IT ITSELF (scripts/verify_infra.sh:87, tools/prep_tcm_node_scst.sh:58), so the 3m39s observation was 1.2 expiries - one decision, timer reset, and the watching stopped before the stack's first real opportunity; and the node that 'could not be unmounted and had to be power-cycled' was inside the 538 s stall when the next prep_cluster ran.
defects.next: 1) THE STALL IS THE DEFECT NOW, and its length is a tunable this project owns: /sys/block/<dev>/device/timeout is 180 s because MXFS's own prep writes it, and three expiries of it is the 538 s. Establish why 180 was chosen before changing it - a shorter command timeout shortens this stall proportionally but makes every transient target hiccup an error, and the fencing design assumes bounded I/O either way. eh_deadline is unset on these nodes and is the other lever: it bounds total error-handler time. 2) WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED: whether a node whose ENTIRE I/O path stalls (rather than one writer's single command) keeps heartbeating for 538 s. This lap showed the heartbeat unaffected because only one task was stranded; a reset landing while the disklock heartbeat's own command is in flight is the case that could cost the node its membership, and it has not been produced. That is the arm that would put this back on the stability bar, and it is the one to run next. 3) DO NOT fix this by making MXFS issue its own reset first, and do not make it a reason to re-enable a retirement assertion. 4) Independent of D-NO-TASK-MANAGEMENT-PATH-...: that one wants to ISSUE a reset; this one is about surviving one issued by anyone.
defects.impact_why: THE 'FOREVER' IS DISPROVED BY DIRECT MEASUREMENT. tests/lu_reset_bystander_eh.sh s84h, 2-node TCP, build 36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343, fails=0 (tests/evidence/20260920T120749Z_lrbe_s84h): ten LOGICAL UNIT RESETs from test1, six seconds apart, with test2 writing O_DIRECT into an MXFS file throughout. Exactly one of the ten stranded a command. test2's writer froze at ok=107910 at t=60s and RESUMED AT t=609s - a 538 s stall, then normal progress, zero application errors. The stack rescued it and narrated doing so: timeouts=7 timer_reset=2 not_handled=1 aborts=3 device_resets=0, and verbatim 'sd 3:0:0:0: [sda] tag#73 aborting command' / 'session1: iscsi_eh_abort abort success [sc ... itt 0x15]' / 'sd 3:0:0:0: [sda] tag#73 retry aborted command'. So there IS a timeout, there IS an abort and there IS a retry, which is the opposite of what this record asserted. 538 s is three expiries of the 180 s device command timeout plus the abort, and the ladder in drivers/scsi/libiscsi.c iscsi_eh_cmd_timed_out gives exactly that: rung 1 answers 'command making progress' and resets the timer, rung 3 sends a nop-out and resets it, and only the pass after that returns SCSI_EH_NOT_HANDLED and lets the error handler in. WHY THE ORIGINAL READING SAID FOREVER: the earlier probe waited 130 s for a writer that needed 538 s, recorded DONE=0, and the next prep_cluster power-cycled the node inside the stall window - both observations are fully explained by a 538 s stall and neither requires a permanent hang. THE DEVICE TIMEOUT IS 180 s, NOT THE 30 s THIS RECORD REASONED FROM, and MXFS sets it itself (scripts/verify_infra.sh:87, tools/prep_tcm_node_scst.sh:58), so the original 3m39s observation was 1.2 expiries - the initiator had made one decision and reset the timer, and the watching stopped before the stack's first real opportunity. NOTHING AT THE STABILITY BAR HAPPENED: zero fence, death-declaration, recovery-pending or self-withdraw lines in EITHER node's kernel window across the whole 1114 s lap; no BUG, no Oops, no filesystem shutdown; both nodes answering at the end; the peer never declared the stalled node dead, because a LU reset strands only the tasks the target held at that instant and the heartbeat's own commands, issued after it, complete normally. The issuing node wrote 217171 blocks with zero errors across the series. No data was lost: the stranded write was retried and completed. What is left is a 538 s stall of one initiator's in-flight I/O, which is the pace axis, and the release bar takes pace off the release path. It stays in the queue at its own severity; it is not a gate.

defects.summary: A durable fence certificate of a class this build has revoked makes the filesystem unmountable on every node, and no operator route to dispose of the record is finished: chk_mxfs --accept-quarantine-loss implements steps 1-4 of its ruling and deliberately stops before the destructive ones.
defects.evidence: MEASURED 2026-09-20 on the 2-node TCP rig, build 36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343, eight arms of tests/fence_kind_matrix.sh (tests/evidence/20260920T113047Z_fkm_s84b_retired16 and seven siblings, each fails=0). A recovery-descriptor certificate of kind 16, 19, 20, 21 or an unknown kind is forged into an unused heartbeat slot by tools/recov_forge with its crc and identity binding recomputed - the shape an older build left on the platter. The mounting node then refuses the claim by class (P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED naming the revoked class verbatim), replays nothing, and the mount ABORTS with rc=32 at 123-124 s. That refusal is CORRECT and is the fix this version shipped; the defect is what happens next. Every subsequent mount of that filesystem, on every node, does the same thing, because the record is durable and nothing removes it. The bound is the mount barrier's own: it prints P-BARRIER-GHOST-EXTEND undeclared=1 window_ms=62000 bound_ms=122000, since a guard slot with no live heartbeat is an undeclared death and buys the one-time extension. THE DISPOSAL ROUTE IS INCOMPLETE, established by reading tools/chk_mxfs.c: do_accept_quarantine_loss's own header states 'THIS BUILD IMPLEMENTS STEPS 1-4 AND STOPS THERE, deliberately' - validate the verdict, take exclusive maintenance ownership, refuse if any non-quarantined slice is dirty, archive off-volume. Steps 5-9 (record LOSS_ACCEPTED, reinitialise the slice, consistency repair, CHECK_COMPLETE, clear the source slot) are unwritten, so the sector is never cleared. It also keys on a QUARANTINED outcome record; a revoked certificate is a live FENCED descriptor with no outcome record at all, so the command does not address this shape even once its remaining steps land.
defects.next: Two separable pieces. (1) THE SHAPE: decide whether a revoked-class certificate is reachable by the same operator route as a quarantined slice, or needs its own. The design ruling docs/rulings/fence-certificate-proof-profiles-and-legacy-revocation.md is explicit that availability does not supply the missing evidence - 'a stranded pending recovery has two options: obtain a new, independently supported proof and issue a new certificate, or stay blocked' - so the route must be an explicit, confirmed ACCEPTANCE OF LOSS, never a relabelling of the certificate and never a silent clear. The forged matrix already proves the refusing path does not rewrite what it refused, which is the invariant any disposal route must not break. (2) THE STEPS: finish chk_mxfs steps 5-9 under the sess377 ruling's ordering, or state in the operator documentation that the only route today is mkfs and that the archive step exists to make that survivable. Do not close this by noting that the refusal is correct: the refusal being correct is why this record exists.
defects.impact_why: Availability, not integrity or stability. Nothing is corrupted - the whole point is that the replay is refused - and nothing hangs or crashes: the mount returns rc=32 at 123-124 s, inside the 122 s bound the barrier prints for itself, and the survivor served throughout every arm (measured, tests/evidence/20260920T113047Z_fkm_s84b_retired16 and seven siblings). What is lost is the ability to mount a filesystem that carries such a record, on every node, permanently. Under the 2-node TCP release bar - 100% data integrity and stability - that does not gate the release. It is in the queue because a fleet upgrading from 0.89.12-0.89.15 with a certificate already on the platter is exactly the population this class of record was retired for.

defects.summary: When a bootstrap-term owner dies and the target has already purged its registration, the takeover correctly refuses to mint a fence kind and returns -ENOKEY before any reseal - so the record is left CLAIMED, owned by a key that can never come back, and every subsequent mount by any node repeats the same contend-wait-refuse. There is no proof-producing transition left, so the volume stays unmountable until an operator runs chk_mxfs --clear-bootstrap.
defects.evidence: REACH CORRECTED 2026-09-20 (0.89.19), same finding as the record this one was split from: THE WHOLE-CLUSTER BOOTSTRAP IS A CAW PATH. v5_bootstrap_run has exactly one call site (dlm/v5_mount.c:16211); the TCP arm of mxfs_v5_dlm_init ends 'return ctx' at :15990 and everything from :15993 is the CAW arm; the tree states it at :15653 ('the TCP transport carries its own durable authority ledger and no PR-fence bootstrap ... bootstrap is a CAW path'). So the refused takeover that leaves the term CLAIMED cannot happen on TCP, because no takeover runs there. MEASURED, twice: tests/bootstrap_takeover_2n.sh s86d and s86e on 2/tcp drove a whole-cluster outage with both slices dirty and one node back; neither reached a claim - the mount took an ordinary heartbeat slot 12 ms after reading the record and was then refused by the admission barrier after 116 and 155 inline replay rounds (tests/evidence/20260920T140746Z_btk_s86d, 20260920T141955Z_btk_s86e). THE INSPECTION EVIDENCE FOR THE CAW PATH IS UNCHANGED: v5_boot_tk_fence_key returns -ENOKEY at P-BOOT-TAKEOVER-FENCE-UNPROVEN when the old owner's key is absent; its caller does 'goto out' BEFORE any lineage write or reseal, so v5_boot_tk_refuse is never reached and nothing durable records the attempt; v5_bootstrap_run returns <0 and the mount is refused with the record still CLAIMED, which is exactly the state that sends the next mount down the same takeover path. THE CROSS-TRANSPORT VARIANT, WHICH A TCP-ONLY DEPLOYMENT CANNOT REACH BUT A MIXED ONE CAN, AND WHICH MUST NOT BE LOST: on TCP the record is still opened (v5_bootstrap_setup) and still read pre-register, and any state that is not IDLE or RECOVERY_COMPLETE refuses the mount with P-BOOT-ADMISSION-REFUSED-PREREGISTER (-EBUSY). Nothing on TCP consumes boot_takeover_pending or boot_resume_pending, so nothing there can advance or clear such a record - and chk_mxfs --clear-bootstrap accepts only a REFUSED record, never a CLAIMED one. A volume left CLAIMED by a CAW mount is therefore unmountable on TCP with no in-product route of any kind. On a volume that has only ever been TCP-mounted the record never leaves the IDLE that mkfs writes.
defects.next: MEASURE IT as part of the 2-node bootstrap-takeover lap: after B's takeover refuses, mount again on B and again on a rebooted A, and show every attempt returns the same refusal with the record unchanged - that is the permanence evidence, and a few repeated mounts alone are not it. THEN FIX, and the ruling is explicit that resealing the owner's record REFUSED from the -ENOKEY exit is NOT the fix: an absent registration does not prove the owner is dead, so that write is an unproved concurrent-writer path, and a one-time CAS does not help if the old owner can later reseal unconditionally. A terminal cancellation protocol needs its own concurrency design (an independently valid atomic conditional transition, protection against the old owner resurrecting the term, every owner publication path respecting the cancellation epoch, a defined treatment of in-flight work, and no reading of the state as fencing proof). The four repair families to weigh: recover and revalidate a genuine durable prior proof covering that exact owner/key/epoch; add a retirement mechanism whose contract covers the outstanding I/O; redesign the ownership protocol so exclusion survives the victim's registration disappearing; or qualify the target profile so the proof operation survives the failure. Note that 'the proof can never arrive' is not 'the proof requirement is satisfied' - no repair may convert impossibility into permission.
defects.impact_why: An ordinary in-scope fault sequence - the first node back after a total outage is power-cut while it holds the bootstrap term - ends with the shared volume unmountable on every node and no automatic path back. The refusal itself is the required safe behaviour and must stay; what crosses the bar is that recovery has no route once the proof is unobtainable. Ruled on-bar by design consult (docs/rulings/bootstrap-takeover-closure-and-the-recovery-dead-end.md, session 86): a declared safety block while proof is unavailable is legitimate, but a persistent dead end after an ordinary fault is a recovery/liveness failure, not a pace defect. Filed from the code path by inspection; the 2-node lap in D-BOOTSTRAP-TAKEOVER-MINTS-... measures it.

defects.summary: A task already parked in a DLM lock request when its mount's authority closes is not aborted by the closure. On 2/tcp: FIXED AND VERIFIED for the acquire wait (0.89.21, 72 s to 3 s) and for the log waits (0.89.67-0.89.69, s150e: closed 25 s, freed 26 s with the PR worker's pump held, converted by the withdraw thread); the closure races and a post-closure grant are settled from the acquire loop's structure. What remains is the CAW transport's own acquire, which has never been measured against a closure.
defects.evidence: ===== THE PUMP IS THE SOLE CONSUMER OF A WITHDRAWAL, PROVEN BY ENUMERATING EVERY READER AND WRITER OF THE FLAG (s129, by reading). This record's next-step said a closure reaches a log shutdown 'solely through v5_authority_withdraw_pump'. That was the right claim but it rested on having found one call; it is now an enumeration over the whole tree and it holds. THE FLAG IS auth->withdraw_pending, declared at dlm/disklock.h:223 with the in-tree comment '/* the pump owes a notify */'. WRITERS - exactly two, and they are the same event: dlm/disklock.c:2443 inside auth_note_closed, which sets close_reason and then withdraw_pending = 1; and dlm/disklock.c:2588, which CLEARS it. auth_note_closed is reached from mxfs_authority_close (dlm/disklock.c:2571-2582) and from the lazy expiry close. mxfs_authority_close ITSELF DOES NOTHING ELSE: its whole body is two cmpxchgs moving the state NOT_ADMITTED->CLOSED or ADMITTED->CLOSED and then the auth_note_closed call - no wake, no waitqueue, no shutdown, nothing that touches a parked task. READERS OF THE FLAG - exactly one that acts on it: mxfs_authority_take_withdraw (dlm/disklock.c:2584-2592), and its ONLY caller in the tree is dlm/v5_mount.c:11546, inside v5_authority_withdraw_pump. THE ONE OTHER WAY IN IS DEAD CODE: mxfs_disklock_authority_take_withdraw (declared dlm/disklock.h:3351, defined dlm/disklock.c:2626-2632) forwards to the same function and HAS NO CALLERS ANYWHERE - the four tree-wide matches for 'authority_take_withdraw' are the two declarations, the two definitions and the single v5_mount.c:11546 call, and nothing else. The module states the design in its own words at dlm/disklock.h:3326: 'raises auth_withdraw_pending and the periodic pump does the notify.' SO THE CHAIN IS SINGLE-THREADED AND IT IS: lease expires or is closed -> auth_note_closed sets withdraw_pending -> the PR worker's 250 ms tick reaches v5_authority_withdraw_pump -> take_withdraw -> fence_notify_fn -> the shutdown that is the ONLY thing that frees a task parked in xlog_grant_head_wait, xlog_wait_on_iclog or xlog_wait_iclog_completion. Remove the pump's tick and there is no other consumer to pick the withdrawal up. THE ONE CLOSURE PATH THAT DOES NOT NEED THE PUMP, and it must not be used to argue the others are safe: v5_resv_conflict_withdraw (dlm/v5_mount.c:11558-11577) calls mxfs_authority_close and then calls ctx->fence_notify_fn ITSELF at :11574-11576, synchronously, in the same function. That is the PR-conflict path only. The AUTHORITY-LEASE-EXPIRED path has no such synchronous notify - that is exactly the asymmetry, and it is why an expired lease and a detected PR conflict do not free a parked task on the same schedule. WHY THIS SHARPENS THE OWED MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN SETTLING IT. The pump's own comment (dlm/v5_mount.c:11537-11540) declares it not load-bearing: 'The gate does not depend on this running. If this worker is stalled too, every mutating submission still refuses on its own; all that is lost is the promptness of the withdrawal.' With the enumeration above, 'all that is lost is promptness' is now demonstrably wrong for one class of caller: a task already parked in a log wait is not a mutating submission being refused, it is asleep, nothing else reads the flag, and the wait's own exits do not include the authority - so for that caller the pump is not promptness, it is the entire mechanism, and a stalled pump is an unbounded uninterruptible wait. THE MEASUREMENT IS UNCHANGED IN SHAPE AND IS NOW EXACTLY SPECIFIED: park a task in one of the three xfs_log.c waits, close authority by letting the lease expire (NOT by a PR conflict, which would take the synchronous path and prove nothing about this one), and measure closed-to-freed twice - once with the PR worker ticking and once with it stalled. The prediction the enumeration makes is that the stalled arm never frees the task at all. NOTHING HERE IS A DISPOSITION: no lap has been run, and a read cannot establish what a live parked task does.
defects.next: ITEM (3) HAS ITS CONTROL MEASUREMENT AND ITS SUBJECT ARM HAS BEEN REBUILT SO IT CAN BE MEASURED AT ALL. The s134 re-run named in the earlier text ran as the s140 pair on build 0.89.6x (tests/evidence/lapq_s140_3.console, lapq_s140_4.console; evidence 20260922T005450Z_plwait_s140c, 20260922T005948Z_plwait_s140d), 2/tcp, with the three harness faults fixed. CONTROL s140c PASS fails=0: the filler parked in xlog_grant_head_wait at +260 s (stack captured), the heartbeat parked 240 s against the 30 s lease, P290-AUTH-CLOSED at 25 s into the window dated by the poker's first EIO at the same second, then P290-AUTH-WITHDRAW, P131-SELF-FENCE and the shutdown, and the parked filler was FREED at 25 s - closed_s=25 freed_s=25, so with the pump running the interval from closure to the parked task's release is below the lap's 1 s resolution. That is the number item (3) asked for on the log wait. defects.summary: mxfs_dlm_lock_retries detects a page transition that has stopped advancing and then, for any caller its acq_fallible_cb does not name, RESETS the stall clock and waits again — so a permanently refused transition is an unbounded kernel wait with no exit but a fatal signal. dlm/dlm.c:8001-8036: on MXFS_DLM_RETRY_TRANSITION the loop compares the takeover's progress counter against trans_prog; MXFS_DLM_TRANSITION_STALL_MS (30000, dlm.c:291) with no advance ends the wait with -EREMCHG ONLY when ctx->acq_fallible_cb says the caller is at a fallible boundary; otherwise it logs P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-STALLED fallible=0, sets trans_t0 = now (dlm.c:8035) and loops, and retries++ at dlm.c:8054 undoes the loop's own budget decrement, so the retry budget is never spent either. The oracle is narrow by construction: v5_acq_fallible_cb (dlm/v5_mount.c:8064-8076) answers 0 for every resource that is not MXFS_LTYPE_AG or MXFS_LTYPE_INODE, and for those two only when the calling TASK registered itself in the XFS layer's per-task registry (mxfs_acq_task_fallible_for / _for_ag). Teardown callers do not register: mxfs_sb_summary_lock (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c:5009-5024) acquires an INODE-type resource on mxfs_sb_summary_key() from xfs_fs_put_super (pal/linux/xfs_super.c:1818) with no registration, so it is permanently non-fallible.
